clinicalPearls: A severe necrotising, gas-forming infection of the renal parenchyma and perirenal tissues, and a urological emergency.
It occurs overwhelmingly in diabetics with poor glycaemic control, and also with urinary tract obstruction.
Escherichia coli is the commonest organism, followed by Klebsiella and Proteus; gas arises from fermentation of glucose and lactate by facultative anaerobes.
It presents as severe pyelonephritis failing to improve, with sepsis; flank crepitus is rare but classic.
Contrast CT is the imaging gold standard, classifying the extent of gas and guiding management.

Management combines aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, glycaemic control and relief of obstruction or percutaneous drainage, with nephrectomy reserved for severe or non-responding disease.
Percutaneous drainage combined with medical therapy has substantially reduced the need for emergency nephrectomy.
Poor prognostic markers include thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, shock, altered consciousness and extensive gas.
reference.pathophysiology: Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a fulminant necrotising infection in which gas-forming facultative anaerobes, chiefly Escherichia coli and Klebsiella, ferment glucose and lactate within poorly perfused, often diabetic renal tissue, generating carbon dioxide and hydrogen that accumulate in the parenchyma, collecting system and perinephric space. High tissue glucose, impaired host defences and reduced perfusion from microvascular disease or obstruction create the anaerobic microenvironment that permits gas production and rapid parenchymal necrosis, with urinary obstruction contributing particularly in non-diabetic cases.
additionalDifferentials: Emphysematous pyelitis (gas confined to the collecting system, better prognosis)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast CT of the abdomen for diagnosis, classification and drainage planning
Blood and urine cultures with sensitivities
Full blood count including platelets, renal function and C-reactive protein
Blood glucose, HbA1c and acid-base and ketone assessment
Serum lactate and markers of sepsis severity
Imaging of the renal tract for obstruction or calculi
Assessment of split renal function if nephrectomy is considered
redFlags: Extensive perinephric or retroperitoneal gas or bilateral disease
reference.prognosis: Historically associated with high mortality, the outlook is now substantially better with early CT diagnosis, prompt drainage and antibiotics, although shock, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment and extensive gas continue to worsen prognosis.
pitfalls: Delaying CT and treating the illness as simple pyelonephritis
Failing to relieve obstruction or drain collections
Defaulting to nephrectomy when drainage would suffice, or conversely delaying it in fulminant disease
management: Aggressive fluid resuscitation and sepsis management, treating the condition as a urological emergency
Early broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and Proteus, later tailored to culture sensitivities
Tight glycaemic control with insulin and correction of acidosis and ketosis
Relief of urinary obstruction and percutaneous drainage of gas and pus collections guided by contrast CT classification, favoured over immediate nephrectomy
Nephrectomy reserved for extensive or non-responding disease and clinical deterioration
Monitoring of renal function, platelet count, serum lactate and sepsis markers for deterioration
Escalation to critical care for shock, with urology and nephrology involvement and follow-up imaging
